title: How Toyota Changed The Way We Make Things
transcript: Toyota knows how to make cars. It does it so well it became the first company to produce more than 10 million a year. Its success is rooted in a special system and began what is now known as ‘Lean Manufacturing’, an ethos emulated by companies around the world to make products faster, cheaper and better. Following the Second World War, Japan was left in a precarious economic position. "Steel and other metals are scarce" Already disadvantaged by lacking natural resources, materials were hard to come by and companies had to be creative to compete. Toyota’s founder Sakichi Toyoda had started a loom business, but it was his son Kiichiro who founded the motor company in 1937. They were used to working within narrow margins - as the shortage of materials increased during the war, the number of headlamps on its Model K truck was reduced to one and it only had brakes on one of the axles. The turning point for Toyota's Production System would come in the early fifties, when Kiichiro's cousin Eiji would travel to the U.S. with a veteran loom machinist, Taiichi Ohno. They visited Ford's River Rouge plant in Michigan and were impressed by the scale of the operation, but knew that in cash-strapped Japan companies didn’t have the resources for such a system; Having months’ worth of stock sitting in a warehouse would tie up precious capital they didn’t have. Instead, what truly impressed Ohno was a visit to a supermarket, a Piggly Wiggly, according to legend... Japan didn’t really have self-service stores at this point - and he was struck by the way customers could choose exactly what they wanted, when they wanted. He decided to model his production line on a similar idea; With a "supermarket formula," only enough parts were produced in the first phase to replace what was used in the second, and so on. This is where the ‘Just In Time’ system really took shape. Toyota was able to eliminate much of the waste in Ford's system, making smaller numbers of parts to be used when it needed them, allowing the company to operate on a tighter budget. As part of this Ohno developed ‘Kanban’ - a sign-based scheduling method which shows goods in, goods in production, and goods out. It’s now seen as a precursor to bar codes. Ohno and Toyoda also noticed that American car companies were still employing many of Henry Ford’s early production techniques - They kept operations at full tilt in order to maximize efficiencies of scale, and then repaired defective cars after they rolled off the line. Ohno believed this caused more problems and didn’t encourage workers, or machines, to stop making the mistake. So he placed a cord above every station which any worker could pull to stop the entire assembly if they spotted a problem. The whole team would work on it, to prevent it from happening again. As teams identified more problems, the number of errors began to drop dramatically. Combined with a culture of continuous, incremental improvement -- called `kaizen' -- the Toyota Production System built a brand known for making reliable and affordable cars. But Toyota was also getting good at producing cars quickly. In 1962, the company had produced one million vehicles. By 1972, they had produced ten million. It was around that time the efficiencies of their factories enabled Toyota to produce a car every 1.6 man hours - much lower than their competitors in the U.S., Sweden and Germany And as the oil crises of the decade sent gas prices higher, cheap-to-run Japanese cars became much more appealing to Americans, whose powerful, but gas-guzzling vehicles suddenly became very expensive to run. Today, Toyota has made over 250 million vehicles… Others have looked to them to learn the lessons of ‘Lean’- combining craft with mass production, avoiding waste, while striving for constant improvement. Boeing is perhaps the most famous, restructuring a plant to better suit TPS. Intel is another long-time lean ambassador, and is exploring the principles in the context of AI and IoT. A Canadian Hospital even used Toyota’s system to decrease wait times in its ER. The Toyota Production System changed not just how cars are made globally but how we approach making things full stop. It also showed there is always a better way to make a product.

title: Lean Manufacturing: What is Lean and the Toyota Production System?
transcript: in this module we will give you a brief introduction to lean first we will answer the question what is lean next we will define the principles and tools of the toyota production system finally we will talk about the benefits of lean transformation james womack was the person who coined the term lean in the book the machine that changed the world which was a study of the automotive industry globally the term lean was used to describe the toyota production system because toyota was able to develop and build better quality automobiles faster than their competition womack defines lean as a systematic approach to identifying and eliminating waste through continuous improvement by flowing the product at the pull of the customer in pursuit of perfection throughout this training we will talk about the principles and tools that will help you transform your organization let's briefly cover where lean came from taiichi ono chief engineer at toyota was faced with the following situation just after world war ii toyota had very little money a very small market productivity 1 10 that of detroit a production requirement of less than 1 100th of ford he was asked to catch up with detroit in just three years that is in terms of productivity while it took longer than that after studying ford and also taking advice from quality gurus such as deming he created a manufacturing system that focused on reducing cost by eliminating waste hence the toyota production system was born the toyota production system is often depicted as a house because it is a structural system rather than simply a set of tools let's take a closer look at this system we'll begin with the goal the goal of lean or the toyota production system is to create the highest quality products at the lowest cost with the shortest lead time to the customer while creating a safe work environment with high employee morale these goals are upheld by two pillars the first pillar is just in time which means providing the next downstream customer with what they need when they need it in the quantity that they need it and at the point in time in which they need it we use several tools and principles to achieve just in time we use continuous flow moving the product from one value-added step to the next with no delay between steps we set our production rate equal to tack time the heartbeat of the customer we use pull systems to build and provide only what the customer needs when they signal for it and we use quick changeover to become more flexible at building what the customer needs when they need it the next pillar is quality at the source this pillar represents the idea that we never knowingly passed effective product to our next downstream customer we prevent this from happening by implementing tools like line stop which empower the operators to stop the line and address a problem when one occurs visual controls to identify problems and prevent problems mistake proofing to prevent human error from causing a defect and on systems light and audible systems to alert us of errors and we employ the concept of the five whys root cause analysis by continually asking the question why until we get to the root cause of a problem rather than addressing symptoms of problems at the base of the toyota production system we have operational stability to create and maintain stable processes we employ standard work which ensures that our process is consistent and able to meet the volume requirements of the customer we employ preventive maintenance or total productive maintenance to ensure that our equipment is reliable and we implement a 5s system to help us organize and standardize our operations and keep it that way finally we employ the concept of hijanka or leveling the workload to ensure a smooth flow of production from beginning to end the final and most important element of lean is to create a flexible capable and highly motivated workforce to make it all happen we want to create a culture of problem solving james womack and daniel jones wrote the book lean thinking back in 1996 to further describe lean in it they identified five principles of lean the first principle of lean is specify value value is what the customer is willing to pay for we need to understand what the customer needs and values first the second principle is identify the value stream we need to identify the value streams for our products or services and then map those value streams to identify waste and sources of waste value streams include all of the actions required to deliver our products or services to our customers next we create continuous or one-piece flow we eliminate delays from our processes in manufacturing this means eliminating work in progress inventory and moving the product from one step to the next with no delay we then employ the concept of pull every point in our process has a customer and we create a system that allows us to only make what the next downstream customer needs finally we pursue perfection we continue to find ways to eliminate waste and improve quality let's take another perspective on lean imagine the timeline that begins with the customer placing an order and ends with the customer paying for that order that timeline includes things like purchasing raw materials manufacturing planning engineering shipping customer service all of the processes necessary to deliver the product or service that timeline includes value creating time time in which you are transforming the product in such a way that the customer is willing to pay for it it also includes non-value creating time time in which no value is being added this represents the time in which the product is waiting taiji ono described the toyota production system this way all we are doing is looking at the timeline from when the customer gives us an order to the point at which we collect the cash and we're reducing that timeline by removing non-value added wastes applying lean principles will create the following types of improvements shorter lead times or turnaround times to customers and faster production lead times or cycle times net decrease in inventory which frees up cash that will be used to fuel growth and pay down debt productivity growth which increases capacity and lowers costs and quality improvement which lowers costs and attracts additional business our operational excellence model begins with strategy deployment originally called hoshin kanri strategy deployment is a methodology used to set the direction of the organization what is our vision what are we trying to achieve and by when which metrics are important for achieving our goals this is an annual process that involves input from all levels of the organization the process results in a clear set of goals breakthrough initiatives and key metrics all aspects of the organization will be rowing in the same direction the next level down is a methodology known as value stream mapping we utilize value stream mapping to further refine our key initiatives a value stream is a way of describing the flow of information and material from customer order or request through to fulfillment of that order or request by analyzing our value streams we can pinpoint specific targeted areas for improvement and develop a plan to make it happen the next two levels are the ways we actually make these things happen to actually make improvements we have several methodologies that we use at the very bottom we have what's called daily kaizen kaizen is a japanese word translating to good change or improvement through daily kaizen each part of our organization is working on reaching particular incremental targets for improvement using scientific thinking many times referred to as a3 thinking or problem solving just one line above daily kaizen are kaizen events and other projects such as damaic projects dimaic is a problem-solving methodology as well which stands for define measure analyze improve and control these team-based activities are used to achieve targeted improvements as well but they are typically reserved for more complicated endeavors this entire model when used correctly allows the organization to learn while changing culture and achieving great gains
